options.C: It can constitute BOTH oppression (prejudicial to members' interests due to value destruction) and mismanagement (prejudicial to the company's interest due to asset stripping), and the application can be brought on both grounds simultaneously
options.D: It constitutes neither oppression nor mismanagement — it is purely a criminal matter under Section 447

questions.explanation: Section 241(1)(a) provides two grounds: (i) affairs conducted in a manner 'prejudicial to the interests of any member' (oppression) and (ii) affairs conducted in a manner 'prejudicial to public interest or the interests of the company' (mismanagement). Siphoning working capital through related-party transactions is prejudicial to both: it destroys shareholder value (oppression) AND depletes the company's assets (mismanagement). An application under Section 241 can invoke both grounds simultaneously. Option D is wrong because the existence of potential criminal liability under Section 447 does not preclude civil remedies under Section 241. The scenario establishes both member harm (value destruction) and company harm (asset stripping).

scenarios.scenarioText: QuickCart E-Commerce Ltd. is a listed public company with 60,000 members, paid-up share capital of ₹500 crore, and 4,000 depositors who have invested ₹200 crore in fixed deposits with the company. In January 2026, a class action was filed under Section 245 by a group of 200 members holding 3% of the issued share capital, alleging that the Board misrepresented the company's user acquisition metrics in the annual report, causing the share price to crash from ₹180 to ₹45 when the truth emerged. The class action also named the company's former CFO, Mr. Nitin Verma (who had resigned 8 months before the crash), and the independent auditor, M/s Kapoor & Sons. Mr. Verma argues that since he resigned before the share price crash, he cannot be held liable. M/s Kapoor & Sons argues that the NCLT has no jurisdiction over audit firms as they are regulated by ICAI. Additionally, a second group of 150 members filed an identical class action 3 months later seeking the same relief against the same respondents. The company's counsel raises the issue of multiplicity of proceedings and argues that the second application should be barred.

questions.question: Mr. Nitin Verma (former CFO) argues that since he resigned 8 months before the share price crash, he cannot be a respondent in the class action. Is this argument valid under Section 245?

options.A: Yes — Section 245 only applies to persons currently holding office in the company at the time the class action is filed
options.B: No — Section 245 covers 'any fraudulent, unlawful or wrongful act or omission or conduct' of the directors/officers; if the wrongful act occurred during Mr. Verma's tenure, his subsequent resignation does not extinguish liability
options.C: Yes — once a person resigns, the NCLT loses personal jurisdiction over them
options.D: No — but only if Mr. Verma resigned less than 6 months before the class action was filed

questions.explanation: Section 245(1)(a) targets 'any fraudulent, unlawful or wrongful act or omission or conduct' of the company or its directors. The misrepresentation of user metrics occurred during Mr. Verma's tenure as CFO. His subsequent resignation does not retroactively extinguish his liability for acts committed while in office. The scenario specifically states the misrepresentation was in the annual report (prepared during his tenure), and the crash merely revealed the pre-existing fraud. Option A is the main trap — Section 245 does not limit respondents to current officers. Option D fabricates a 6-month limitation that does not exist in the statute.

questions.question: M/s Kapoor & Sons argues that as an audit firm regulated by ICAI, the NCLT has no jurisdiction over them in a class action. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: The argument is valid — auditors are exclusively regulated by ICAI and NFRA, and the NCLT cannot exercise jurisdiction over them
options.B: The argument is invalid — Section 245(1)(c) specifically includes 'the auditor including audit firm of the company' as a respondent in class actions, and the NCLT's jurisdiction under Section 245 is independent of ICAI's regulatory jurisdiction
options.C: The argument is partially valid — the NCLT can hear the case but cannot impose any penalty on the audit firm
options.D: The argument is valid — but only for audit firms; individual auditors can be respondents

questions.explanation: Section 245(1)(c) explicitly includes 'the auditor including audit firm of the company' as a proper respondent. The words 'including audit firm' leave no ambiguity — both individual auditors and audit firms can be sued in class actions. ICAI's regulatory jurisdiction over professional conduct is separate from the NCLT's statutory jurisdiction under Section 245. The two operate in parallel — ICAI can impose professional penalties while the NCLT can order compensation, restraints, and other civil remedies. Option D is wrong because the statute specifically includes 'audit firm.' The scenario's emphasis on M/s Kapoor & Sons certifying falsified accounts is a textbook case for auditor liability under Section 245.

questions.question: A second group of 150 members filed an identical class action 3 months after the first group's application. Under Section 245, what is the likely treatment of this second application?

options.A: The second application must be admitted independently — every group has an independent right to file a class action
options.B: Section 245(4) provides that where a class action application has been filed, no other class action application shall be permitted on the same cause of action — the second application is barred
options.C: The second group must join the first application as co-petitioners or interveners
options.D: Both applications proceed simultaneously and the Tribunal consolidates them at the final hearing stage

questions.explanation: Section 245(4) provides a clear bar against multiplicity: where an application has been filed under Section 245, no other application by the same or different group on the same cause of action shall be permitted. The second group's application — seeking the same relief against the same respondents on the same facts — is barred. This prevents duplicative litigation and ensures that the first class action represents all affected members. The binding effect under Section 245(7) means the first class action's outcome will bind all members anyway, making a second application redundant. The company's counsel is correct on this point.

questions.question: Regarding the binding effect of the class action order, which of the following statements about Section 245(7) is INCORRECT?

options.A: The order is binding on the company and all its members
options.B: The order is binding on all depositors of the company
options.C: The order is binding only on those members who were parties to the class action and who actively participated in the proceedings
options.D: The order is binding on all persons associated with the company including directors and officers

questions.explanation: Section 245(7) provides that any order passed by the Tribunal 'shall be binding on the company and on all its members, depositors and other persons associated with the company.' The order is binding on ALL members — not just those who participated. Option C states the order binds only participating members, which is INCORRECT and therefore the answer. This 'in rem' binding effect is the essence of a class action — it prevents individual members from re-litigating the same issues. In the QuickCart scenario, all 60,000 members are bound by the order, whether they supported it, opposed it, or were completely unaware of it.

questions.question: The company's Board wants to withdraw the class action by passing a Board resolution and offering an out-of-court settlement to the 200 members who filed. Can the Board unilaterally dispose of the class action in this manner?

options.A: Yes — the Board can settle any litigation by passing a resolution and offering compensation to the applicants
options.B: Yes — but only with the approval of shareholders in general meeting by ordinary resolution
options.C: No — Section 245(8) provides that no class action application can be withdrawn or settled without the approval of the Tribunal
options.D: No — class actions cannot be withdrawn or settled under any circumstances; they must proceed to final adjudication

questions.explanation: Section 245(8) provides that no application filed under Section 245 shall be withdrawn without the leave (approval) of the Tribunal. Similarly, any settlement of a class action requires Tribunal approval. This prevents the respondent company from pressuring applicant members into withdrawing through private settlements that may not serve the interests of the wider class. The Board cannot unilaterally dispose of the class action by offering a settlement to just the 200 filing members — since the order binds all 60,000 members (Section 245(7)), any settlement must protect all affected members and requires Tribunal scrutiny. Option D is too extreme — settlement is possible but only with Tribunal approval.
